title: How to Open Your Home in Hospitality as a Family
excerpt: Hospitality is not entertaining. It is opening your ordinary home to people who need it, and letting your children grow up watching the table get longer.
body:
We have confused hospitality with entertaining, and the confusion has emptied our homes. Entertaining is about the host: the clean house, the impressive meal, the performance that leaves guests admiring you. It is exhausting, expensive, and exclusive, reserved for people who are easy to host and rooms that are ready to be seen. So most families do it rarely, if at all, and the door stays shut.

Hospitality is something else entirely. The word in the New Testament is philoxenia, love of the stranger, the literal opposite of xenophobia. It is not about the host at all. It is about the guest, and especially the guest who has nothing to give back. Hospitality opens an ordinary home, with its ordinary mess and its ordinary food, to people who need a place at a table. A family that learns this gives its children one of the deepest formations there is.

## Why hospitality is a command, not a hobby

The early church was built on open homes. They had no buildings; they met in houses, and the practice of taking in strangers and travelers was so central that it appears again and again in the commands of the New Testament. "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." "Practice hospitality." It is not presented as a gift for the outgoing or a hobby for those with nice homes. It is presented as a duty of the ordinary Christian household, yours included.

And it runs back further. Israel was commanded to love the foreigner, to leave the edges of the field for the stranger and the poor, because they themselves had been strangers in Egypt. The whole posture of God's people toward the outsider is welcome, rooted in the memory of having been welcomed first. A family that opens its home is teaching its children the gospel in physical form: you were a stranger, and you were taken in.

## Start with what you have

The great barrier is the lie that you must be ready. The house is not clean enough, the food is not good enough, the budget will not stretch. Refuse the lie. Hospitality is offered from the home you actually have, and the willingness to let people see your real life, dishes in the sink and all, is itself a gift. It tells the guest: you do not have to be impressive here either.

Start small. Invite one person or one family for a simple meal. Make the food you would make for yourselves and set an extra place. The goal is not a performance the guest admires. It is a table where the guest belongs. Some of the most formative hospitality is the least impressive: a bowl of soup, a crowded kitchen, a guest who stayed too long and was glad to.

## Welcome the ones who cannot pay you back

Jesus said something direct and uncomfortable about this. When you give a feast, do not invite only the people who will invite you back. Invite the poor, the ones who cannot repay you. The whole logic of hospitality bends toward the person who has nothing to give in return, because that is exactly how God has been hospitable to us.

So widen the table beyond your own circle. The lonely person from church who is always alone on holidays. The new family who knows no one. The college student far from home. The neighbor in a hard stretch. Let your children grow up watching their parents seek out the overlooked and set a place for them. That sight will form their hearts more than any lesson on loving the poor, because they will have seen it done in their own kitchen.

## Give your children a role

Hospitality is not something the parents do while the children are managed out of the way. Bring them into it. Let them help cook, set the table, answer the door, take a coat. Let them learn to ask a guest about themselves and actually listen. A child who is given a real part in welcoming people becomes an adult for whom an open home is simply normal.

This is messy, and the welcome will not be smooth, and a young child will say the wrong thing to a guest. Let it be imperfect. The guest who needs welcome is not looking for polish. They are looking for a place where they are wanted, and a child's clumsy delight in their arrival often gives that better than any adult performance.

## Count the cost honestly

Hospitality costs. It costs money you would rather save, time you would rather keep, and privacy you would rather hold. The home becomes less yours and more available, and that is precisely the point. A family that never opens its home keeps its life tidy and small. A family that opens its home repeatedly pays a real price and gains a thing money cannot buy: children who know in their bodies that the table is meant to get longer, not the door to stay shut.

I have kept my door closed out of fatigue and the wish to be left alone, telling myself I would open it in a better season. The better season is a fiction. The home is opened in the tired, ordinary present or it is not opened at all.

## This week

This week, invite one person or family who would not expect it, especially someone who cannot easily pay you back, for a simple meal in your ordinary home. Do not clean for a performance and do not cook to impress. Make what you would eat anyway and set an extra place. Give each of your children a real job in the welcome. Then sit, and stay at the table longer than is efficient, and let your children see what it looks like when the door of a Christian home is open.

You are teaching them, with the most ordinary tools you own, that they were strangers once, and they were taken in.
